extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, philosophy of science, and logic
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for forming, testing, and accepting scientific hypotheses (the hypothetical method, induction, verification, and vera causa). Applies to judging whether a hypothesis legitimately counts as proved or only as conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of the Hypothetical Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hypothetical Method suppresses the induction-to-ascertain-law step and contents itself with ratiocination and verification; it is legitimate only if the verification amounts to, and fulfills the conditions of, a complete induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is realized when the case is such that a false law cannot lead to the true result — i.e., when no law except the assumed one can deductively lead to the same conclusions. Example: Newton's assumptions about central force were legitimate because alternative hypotheses could be shown inconsistent with Kepler's laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference / Requirement of Both Instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification must furnish both the affirmative instance (A B C => a b c) and the negative instance (B C => b c) required by the Method of Difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is necessary to be able to obtain, by deduction or experiment, the negative instance showing that no antecedent except the one assumed would, with B C, produce a. Newton obtained the negative instance by showing any other direction of force would not yield equal areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness (No Other Hypothesis Produces Same Results)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis can be treated as inductively proved only when it can be shown that no other hypothesis would account for the phenomena in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The assurance that a hypothesis is true depends on demonstrating that different suppositions could not lead to identical consequences; if multiple distinct hypotheses could produce the same observed results, the assumed one is not thereby proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera Causa / Testability of the Supposed Cause
rubrics_metrics.description: When a hypothesis relates to causation, the supposed cause should be a real phenomenon and should be capable of being detected and proved by independent evidence (a 'vera causa').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the cause be already known, but its existence and connection with the effect must be capable, in principle, of being demonstrated independently. Hypotheses suggesting causes that cannot be independently evidenced are only plausible conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses as Heuristic / Provisional Role
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are indispensable provisional suppositions that suggest lines of investigation and experiments; they enable science to move forward toward more certain results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even false or rudely-corrected hypotheses are useful because they indicate experiments to try and are iteratively refined until deductive results tally with phenomena. Newton's 'Hypotheses non fingo' did not imply shunning provisional assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testability Requirement — Hypotheses Must Be Falsifiable by Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: A sound scientific hypothesis must be of such a nature that it can be either proved or disproved by comparison with observed facts; if it cannot be so tested it should not be accepted as true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses like Descartes' vortices were defective because they could not be brought to the test of observation; the free passage of comets served to disprove vortices because they made observable predictions that failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive Success Is Not Conclusive Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The coincidence of predictions with subsequent observations increases plausibility but does not amount to conclusive proof of a hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a hypothesis anticipates new phenomena (e.g., undulatory theory predicted certain interference effects), such coincidences may only show partial identity of laws and do not prove the underlying mechanism, because different mechanisms can share laws or be modified to fit facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Deductive Derivation of Instances (including Negative Ones)
rubrics_metrics.description: It suffices that we can obtain assurance that A B C will produce a b c, and B C will produce b c, whether by experiment or prior deduction; the nature of the evidence for these instances is immaterial so long as we have the assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some cases, as with Newton, the necessary instances are produced by deduction from the hypothesis rather than by direct experiment; this still can fulfill the conditions of the Method of Difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction Between Descriptive Laws and Causal Hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses that merely describe laws of correspondence between observed facts (without asserting causation) can be accepted as true if verification shows they accord with phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Kepler's empirical laws and hypotheses about the form of planetary orbits: when such suppositions are verified by facts, verification is proof even absent causal attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of Multiple, Modifiable Hypotheses (Ad hoc Rescue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept a hypothesis as true simply because no other hypothesis is currently imagined; alternative unknown causes might exist and hypotheses can often be successively modified to fit facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Whewell's claim that fitting phenomena implies truth is criticized because exploded hypotheses could be modified to coincide with facts; the inability to imagine alternatives is not evidence of uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of Simplicity and Iterative Correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with the simplest supposition consistent with obvious facts; trace consequences, compare with observed facts, and iteratively correct the hypothesis until deductive results match phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The simplest supposition is preferred because its consequences are easiest to trace; tentative, successive corrections are part of a method analogous to mathematical approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of Reasoning from Present Effects to Past Causes (Circumstantial Inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When known laws and agents are invoked to infer past causes from present effects (e.g., geology, judicial inference), such inferences are legitimate provided no other known cause could have generated the effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operation differs from inventing new agencies; it relies on uniformities established by induction and is acceptable even when direct proof of the agent's presence in the past is lacking, so long as alternatives are excluded.
